question: How well can differences in investment, schooling and working-age population growth account for international differences in 1985 output per working-age person and in its growth from 1960 to 1985? Compare economies in which physical capital alone can be accumulated with economies in which both physical and human capital can be accumulated. Can the same assumptions account for the magnitudes of income differences, the pace of adjustment and international differences in returns to investment?

conditions.production: In continuous time, let Y = K^α H^β (AL)^(1−α−β), where K and H are physical and human capital, L is labor and A is labor efficiency. Factors receive their marginal products. Study α > 0 with β = 0 and with β > 0.
conditions.accumulation: Each active stock starts positive, receives a strictly positive constant country-specific fraction of output and depreciates at the common rate δ. The investment fractions sum to less than one. A unit of output can finance a unit of consumption or of either investment good.
conditions.growth_rates: L and A grow at constant annual rates n and g. Allow n to vary by country, take g and δ as common, and assume n + g + δ > 0. Use g + δ = 0.05 for empirical calibration, with g = 0.02 and δ = 0.03 where the split matters.
conditions.productivity: Initial log efficiency has a common component and a persistent country component. State the identification assumptions needed for each use of the cross section.
conditions.returns_regimes: Analyze α + β < 1 and the boundary α + β = 1. For the boundary illustration use constant technology with a common positive multiplier B in Y = B K^α H^(1−α).
conditions.share_benchmarks: Use α = 1/3 as an illustrative physical-capital share. For a rough independent benchmark for human capital, take unskilled earnings to be 30–50% of the average manufacturing wage. For a numerical transition comparison use n + g + δ = 0.06 with α = 1/3 and β equal to zero or one third.
conditions.education_measurement: The dictionary gives the construction of the enrollment measure. Consider both proportional and general log-linear links between enrollment and resources invested in education. For one output-accounting exercise, assume the entire human-capital investment flow is omitted from recorded GDP.
conditions.observations: Use the supplied historical sample flags, endpoint incomes per person aged 15–64, period averages, percent units and missing-value conventions. The separate GDP growth field measures aggregate output growth.
conditions.return_illustrations: For a steady-state net physical-return calibration use the intermediate sample and α = 1/3. For a separate comparison across income levels away from steady state, assume common productivity levels and equal marginal returns across active capital stocks within each economy.

data_access_status: The rounded country cross section and its definitions are supplied. They support the income-level, growth, graphical and model-based return analyses. Historical working files, annual investment paths, capital stocks, observed yields and profits, domestic saving and international flows, nationalization and compensation records, and earnings histories are unavailable.
required_outputs: Derive the stock dynamics and determine whether interior stationary allocations exist and how economies starting from positive stocks behave. Derive implications for income, factor shares and the interpretation of holding a stock or an investment rate fixed. Assess the enrollment measure, the consequences of omitted inputs and the effect of the stated GDP accounting convention.

Evaluate both models against final income in each historical sample. Derive and test their quantitative restrictions, compare fit with the plausibility of the implied shares, and examine empirically whether the education measure matters for interpreting the other inputs. Report sample sizes, intercepts, slopes, standard errors, adjusted fit, residual scale, restriction-test results and implied parameters with uncertainty wherever applicable.

Derive local and finite-horizon income dynamics. Work out the speed and half-life of adjustment where defined. Use the benchmarks to compare magnitudes. At the returns boundary, analyze the capital mix, balanced growth, sensitivity to saving and the relevance of initial imbalances. Distinguish aggregate growth, growth per worker and the contribution of depreciation.

Use the endpoints to investigate catch-up across all three samples. Examine whether the comparison depends on what determines long-run income. Test the transition implications of both technologies, quantify annual adjustment and structural shares where identified, and provide graphical evidence on the relation between initial income and subsequent growth. Explain how country variation in n bears on any sample-wide speed and justify the uncertainty reported.

Derive model-implied returns and report the mean and standard deviation of the calibrated net physical return. Analyze how the income–return relationship away from steady state depends on factor shares. Assess the historical comparisons involving financial yields and capital movements, productive capital and factor shares, expropriation and compensation, and earnings gains from schooling. Identify the observable comparison and the evidence available or missing in each case.

Reconcile the evidence on levels, transitions and returns. Discuss sample selection, persistent productivity differences, measured productivity, private and social returns, and the determinants left outside the models. Include a country appendix preserving all supplied observations, historical membership flags, units and blanks.
source_restrictions: Use only the two named files and the stated primitives. Develop the derivations and empirical design independently. No outside search, source retrieval, published results, replication code or additional datasets.
neutrality_obligation: Report the direction, magnitude, fit and precision supported by the analysis, including differences across samples. Distinguish assumptions, estimates, model predictions and historical observations. State where evidence is insufficient and keep those comparisons in the assessment.
